content: 1. Solids accumulate in pits at an average rate of 40 to 60 liters per person per year, and this can increase to 90 liters per person per year if dry cleansing materials like leaves or paper are used. 2. In emergency situations, toilets with infiltrating pits often experience heavy usage. This can necessitate manual or pour-flush emptying and transportation of fecal sludge to a treatment facility. 3. Fecal sludge, once treated, can be repurposed as a soil conditioner, solid fuel, or building material. Effluent, after treatment, can be used for irrigation or surface water recharge. 4. The rate of accumulation of excreta and cleansing materials in pits often exceeds the rate of decomposition, leading to a potential 50% increase in the normal accumulation rate. 5. Pits should be designed to hold at least 1,000 liters, with a typical depth of at least 3 meters and a diameter of around 1 meter. Pits deeper than 5 meters carry a higher risk of collapse. 6. Depending on usage and depth, some pits may last over 20 years without requiring emptying, while shallow pits used by many people daily may need to be emptied once or twice a year. 7. A pit used by a family of six, with a diameter of 1.5 meters, will likely require emptying after approximately 15 years. 8. Reusable pits should be lined with materials such as brick, rot-resistant timber, concrete, stones, or mortar plastered onto the soil. However, if the soil is stable and free of sand, gravel, or loose organic materials, the entire pit may not need lining. 9. The bottom of the pit should remain unlined to allow liquid infiltration, but the water table and groundwater usage must be considered to avoid contaminating drinking water sources. 10. If groundwater is not used for drinking or alternative cost-effective water sources are available, these options should be explored before assuming pit latrines pose a groundwater contamination risk. 11. Pits should be installed in areas downgradient of drinking water sources and at a minimum horizontal distance of 15 meters from them. 12. Only excreta, cleansing water, flush water, and dry cleansing materials should be introduced into the system. Other inputs, such as menstrual hygiene products and solid wastes, can significantly increase pit contents and complicate emptying. 13. To prevent rapid filling and facilitate emptying, appropriate containers for disposing of non-degradable waste should be provided in toilet cubicles. 14. Some greywater in the pit may aid degradation, but excessive amounts can lead to rapid filling and/or excessive leaching. 15. Untreated fecal sludge is highly pathogenic, and direct human contact or agricultural application should be avoided. Instead, it should be transported to a fecal sludge treatment facility. 16. Conveyance technologies for sludge include manual or motorized emptying and transport. However, vacuum trucks are unsuitable as they can only handle liquid sludge. 17. If a treatment facility is not easily accessible, sludge can be discharged to a transfer station and then transported to the treatment facility using motorized transport. 18. Treatment technologies produce both effluent and sludge, which may require further treatment before end use or disposal. Effluent can be co-treated with wastewater in stabilization ponds or constructed wetlands and then used for irrigation, fish ponds, or surface water recharge. 19. Treated sludge can be used in agriculture as a soil conditioner, as a solid fuel, or as an additive to construction materials. 20. Users are typically responsible for constructing toilets and pits, often hiring masons for the work. They are also responsible for cleaning and repairing the toilet, including the slab, seat/squat hole, drop-hole, cover/lid, and superstructure. 21. In rural areas, users may empty pits themselves, but in urban areas, this is more likely to be done by service providers who charge households for the service. 22. At shared facilities, designated individuals should be identified to clean and maintain the toilets on behalf of all users. 23. Conveyance and treatment technologies are usually operated and maintained by a combination of private and public service providers. For example, private or public providers may handle emptying and transport, while public providers operate treatment plants. 24. All tools and equipment used in conveyance and treatment require regular maintenance by the relevant service providers. 25. Farmers and the general public are the primary users of treated products and are responsible for maintaining the tools and equipment they use. 26. Toilets and pits isolate excreta and pathogens from human contact, preventing disease transmission. During rains, they contain fresh excreta and prevent it from being washed into surface water bodies. 27. Squat-hole covers or lids reduce disease transmission by preventing vectors from entering and leaving the pit. 28. Leachate from pits infiltrates surrounding soil, where pathogens are filtered out, adsorbed onto particles, or die off during slow travel through the soil. 29. The conveyance step removes pathogen hazards from the local community. Workers involved in emptying and transport must wear personal protective equipment and follow standard operating procedures. 30. Workers should not enter pits but use long-handled shovels to remove sludge. Non-degradable solid waste removed from pits must be disposed of properly, either through regulated waste management services or burial. 31. Treatment plants must be securely fenced to prevent unauthorized access. Workers must wear protective equipment and follow standard procedures to safeguard their health. 32. Properly designed, constructed, and operated treatment technologies can reduce pathogen hazards in effluent or sludge to levels appropriate for intended end use or disposal. 33. Sludge requires dewatering and drying before use as a soil conditioner, while for use as solid fuel or building material additives, only dewatering and drying are needed. 34. Effluent requires stabilization and pathogen inactivation in ponds or wetlands before use as irrigation water. 35. End users must wear protective equipment and follow standard procedures to protect themselves, colleagues, and the public when handling treated products. 36. Biogas reactors collect, store, and treat excreta while producing biogas for cooking, lighting, or electricity generation. They can also process organic waste and animal waste. 37. Biogas reactors require pour-flush or urine-diverting flush toilets. Urine-diverting systems allow urine to be stored separately for agricultural use as a nutrient source. 38. Sludge from biogas reactors is not pathogen-free and must be removed cautiously and transported for further treatment. 39. Biogas must be consistently used to prevent pressure buildup, which can force partially digested sludge out of the tank. 40. Biogas reactors are suitable for rural and peri-urban areas with space, organic substrate availability, and uses for biogas and digestate. 41. Proper sludge management is essential in urban areas, as digestate production is continuous and requires regular emptying and transport. 42. Biogas reactors can handle a wide range of inputs, but care must be taken not to overload the system with excessive solids or liquids. 43. Greywater should not be added to biogas reactors as it reduces hydraulic retention time. A separate greywater system is required. 44. Digestate should not be applied directly to agriculture but transported to a sludge treatment facility. 45. Biogas reactors are cost-intensive but can be shared among households. Maintenance costs depend on the frequency and method of emptying. 46. Toilets connected to biogas reactors should be made of durable materials like concrete or stainless steel and designed to prevent stormwater infiltration. 47. Achieving a balance between excreta, organics, and water in biogas reactors may take time, but the system is generally forgiving.
